\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:hi-please}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please in Hindi, both with \hi{कृपया} and with the polite verb ending everyday speech actually prefers.}

Say \hi{कृपया} with its vocalic \hi{ऋ}, unpack it as 'of your compassion', then switch to the everyday \hi{बैठिए}, 'please sit'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṛpayā]{\hi{कृपया} (kṛpayā) — please (kindly)}

\label{lesson:HI-C08-kripaya}



\begin{quote}
Hindi's dictionary word for \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} is really the word \textbf{compassion} in disguise — and it's more formal than you might expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} = \textbf{please}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{kindly / graciously}.\textquotedblright{} It's built on the Sanskrit noun \textbf{\hi{कृपा}} (\emph{kṛpā}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{grace, compassion, mercy}\textquotedblright{} — so asking with \emph{kṛpayā} means, at heart, \textquotedblleft{}of your compassion.\textquotedblright{}

That places Hindi in good company: \textbf{Arabic} asks \emph{min faḍlik} (\textquotedblleft{}from your \textbf{grace}\textquotedblright{}), and the Dravidian languages ask with \emph{daya} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{compassion}\textquotedblright{}). A whole swathe of Asia says \emph{please} by naming the kindness it hopes for — a different instinct from French's \textquotedblleft{}if it \textbf{pleases} you.\textquotedblright{}

The first letter hides a sound you met in the syllabary track: \textbf{\hi{कृ}} is \emph{ka} carrying the \textbf{vocalic r} (the \emph{\hi{ृ}} mark) — \emph{kṛ}, the same \emph{ṛ} vowel Sanskrit and the Dravidian scripts share.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about how it's used}
Here's the catch a textbook often hides: \textbf{\hi{कृपया} is formal and bookish.} You'll see it on signs and hear it in announcements (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{kṛpayā} mind the gap\textquotedblright{}), but in everyday speech Hindi speakers rarely say it. Real politeness usually rides on \textbf{the verb} instead — the respectful request ending \textbf{‑\hi{इए} / ‑\hi{इएगा}} (\emph{-iye / -iyegā}): \emph{baiṭh\textbf{iye}} \textquotedblleft{}please sit,\textquotedblright{} \emph{sun\textbf{iye}} \textquotedblleft{}please listen.\textquotedblright{} And very often, people simply say the English word \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{}}

So learn \emph{kṛpayā} to \textbf{read} it and to be formally polite — but know that the living \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} of Hindi is baked into the verb.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṛpayā\textquotedblright{} — kṛ with the vocalic r, then -payā
  \item the root — \textquotedblleft{}kṛpā = compassion\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}of your compassion\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday way — the verb ending: \textquotedblleft{}baiṭhiye\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the formal Hindi word for please? (\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} \emph{kṛpayā}.) What does its root \emph{kṛpā} mean, and which other languages ask the same way? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Grace / compassion\textquotedblright{}} — like Arabic \emph{min faḍlik} and Dravidian \emph{daya}.) Is \emph{kṛpayā} what people usually say out loud? (\textbf{No} — it's formal; everyday politeness rides on the verb ending \emph{-iye/-iyegā}, or people say English \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
